source.title: PHEW: Paths with higher edge-weights give "winning tickets" without training data

record.file_problem: The supplied text appears to contain the full paper; no truncation or garbling noted.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports a qualitative training-error comparison for sparse convolutional networks, but does not report terminal training classification error.
record.gate_note: Most results compare test accuracy, path-kernel trace, or network width and do not measure the claim's training-error outcome. The one text-described training-error comparison is included; figure-only accuracy results are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study uses Kaiming initialization and batch normalization in evaluating sparse-network construction methods. Its own results concern pruning performance, test accuracy, architecture and early convergence. It does not measure near-zero terminal training error, teacher-student local minima, depth degradation, initialization-dependent training speed or depth, stability thresholds, or a normalization comparison.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that maximizing path-kernel trace produces narrow sparse networks, whereas PHEW combines high trace with preserved layer width and improves test performance over the tested data-independent pruning baselines.
record.recipe_differences: The study constructs sparse subnetworks at initialization using weight-biased random walks and compares their subsequent training; it does not test the claim's general training recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that training error falls faster initially for PHEW than for unbiased and inverse-weight-biased walks; it also reports accuracy robustness across several initializations, but those accuracy results do not measure the listed versions.

fits_no_version.finding: PHEW training error decreases faster initially than with uniform or inverse-weight-biased random walks, approximately during epochs 1–20.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Selecting higher-magnitude weights when constructing sparse networks can accelerate early training relative to alternative random-walk selection rules.

fits_no_version.finding: PHEW test accuracy is reported as robust across Kaiming, normal and Xavier uniform initialization; reinitialized PHEW networks retain similar performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: PHEW's final generalization performance is robust to the tested initialization and reinitialization schemes.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing sparse-network layer width while preserving layer-wise parameter counts improves reported classification performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Wider sparse convolutional networks can generalize better at fixed layer-wise parameter counts.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 38th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 139, 2021
record.problems: The training-error comparison is qualitative, covers only early epochs, and gives no terminal training-error values or uncertainty for that measure.
record.rows_left_out: Test-accuracy, width, and path-kernel-trace results in Figures 1–13 were left out because they do not measure training classification error reaching zero or near zero.

untested.parts: Zero or near-zero training classification error on CIFAR-10/100, including corrupted labels, and the stated exceptions.
Spurious-local-minimum frequency and the effect of adding student neurons in two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems.
Training-error degradation with depth and its prevention by identity shortcuts or special initialization.
Activation-matched initialization effects on training speed and trainable depth, signal and gradient preservation, and orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization.
Loss and curvature dynamics relative to learning-rate stability thresholds.
Training speed and learning-rate tolerance with versus without batch normalization, including the Fixup comparison.

record.verdict_notes: Initialization robustness is measured through final accuracy, not training speed or trainable depth. Width comparisons do not measure spurious local minima in the teacher-student setting. Neither result supports or challenges the corresponding claim versions.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not report whether training classification error reaches zero or near zero, nor results for corrupted or random labels, smaller models, early stopping, or regularized recipes.

rows.subject: PHEW networks
rows.size_stated: ResNet20 and VGG19 are named in the surrounding ablation discussion; exact model association for this training-error statement is not stated.
rows.operation_detail: Compared training-error decrease against unbiased and inverse-weight-biased random-walk variants.

conditions.value: CIFAR-10/100 in the surrounding ablation study; exact dataset association for this statement is not stated

rows.measure: Training error decreases faster initially for PHEW than for the two variants; no numeric values or terminal error are given.
rows.baseline: Unbiased and inverse-weight-biased random-walk variants; numeric baseline not stated.
rows.note: The paper gives a qualitative early-epoch comparison only, so this result cannot establish whether training error ultimately reaches near zero.
rows.check: This is a qualitative comparison of the authors' pruning method with its variants over approximately epochs 1–20. Faster initial training-error decrease cannot establish V1's zero or near-zero terminal training classification error. It also does not test V4's activation-matched initialization mechanism. The exact architecture and dataset for this observation are unspecified; it should not be a claim-evidence row.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
